transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Hi, doctor. Thank you for seeing me. Well, it's... it's really been building up for a while now, but what finally pushed me to actually come in and do something about it is my work. I'm a medical services manager, I oversee a pretty busy outpatient clinic, so as you can imagine, my days are just packed with administrative tasks. And I've always been able to handle it, I know the systems, but lately... well, take our reporting, for example. 

I can start pulling an EPIC quality report—and you probably know how tedious EPIC can be with all the different modules and data fields—and I will sit down at my desk with absolutely every intention of tracking it all, getting the data sorted for our quarterly review. I tell myself, 'Okay, focus, get this done.' But within just a few minutes, my mind has drifted so far away that I’ll suddenly realize I’m just rereading the exact same column of numbers over and over, and none of it is actually registering in my brain. 

It happens in person, too. I'll sit down in a big clinic metrics meeting, pen in hand, ready to go over the patient flow data, and then I don't know, a little while later I'll snap back to reality and realize I completely missed the whole point of the discussion. The department heads will be talking about a new protocol, and my brain was just... somewhere else entirely. It's embarrassing, really, because I'm supposed to be the one leading these initiatives and keeping everyone on track, but I just can't seem to stay locked in on the information right in front of me.
Do you feel anxious when you find your mind drifting away from tasks or meetings?

Anxious? Well... I don't know if "anxious" is the right word, really. It's more like... well, it's incredibly frustrating, I can tell you that much. When I realize I've drifted off, it's not a panicky feeling, it's more of a sinking feeling. Like, "Oh great, here we go again." I mean, I don't sit there with my heart racing or sweating or anything like that. It's just... I'll be in the middle of looking at those EPIC reports—and like I said, they are so detailed, you really have to pay attention to every little cell in the spreadsheet, especially when you're looking at the patient flow metrics for the whole quarter—and when I snap back and realize I haven't actually absorbed a single thing for the last ten minutes, I just feel annoyed with myself. 

And in the meetings, it's the same thing. I don't feel nervous beforehand, and I don't feel scared when I drift off. I just feel... embarrassed, I guess? When someone asks me a question and I have to ask them to repeat it because I was completely zoned out, thinking about something completely unrelated, like whether I need to pick up dry cleaning or something trivial. But anxiety? No, I wouldn't say I feel anxious about it. Just really, really tired of it happening. It's like my brain just refuses to cooperate, no matter how much I tell it to focus. So, no, not anxious. Just... defeated sometimes, I suppose.
Do you often feel sad or down, especially when you're not in the middle of one of these episodes where your mind drifts away?

Sad? No, I really wouldn't say I feel sad or down. I mean, sure, like I was saying, it's incredibly frustrating when I can't seem to get my brain to just stay on track during a meeting or when I'm staring at those endless EPIC spreadsheets. That can make me feel a bit defeated in the moment, absolutely. But it doesn't linger like a dark cloud over my whole life, if that makes sense. 

I'm actually a pretty upbeat person generally. I love my job—well, most parts of it, anyway, when I'm not fighting my own attention span. I have a good life outside of the clinic, too. I like being active, I have friends I see regularly. I don't sit at home crying or feeling hopeless or anything like that. It's not a pervasive sadness. It's really just this very specific, very localized annoyance with my own cognitive functioning, I guess you could call it. 

Like, if I manage to actually get through a whole morning without zoning out during a critical budget review—which, honestly, is rare these days, but when it happens—I feel great! I feel accomplished and completely normal. It's only when the... the drifting happens that I get down on myself. But even then, it's not like a clinical depression kind of sadness. It's more like, "Come on, pull it together, you're fifty years old and you've been doing this job for years, why is this suddenly so hard?" But no, I don't walk around feeling sad or blue most of the time. Not at all.
Have you been having trouble sleeping?

Sleep? No, I wouldn't say I've been having trouble sleeping. I mean, I go to bed around the same time every night, usually right after I finish up whatever reading I brought home from the clinic—which, let's be honest, usually takes me twice as long as it should because of the whole drifting off thing I was telling you about. But once I actually turn the light off and put my head on the pillow, I'm out pretty quickly. 

I don't lie there tossing and turning, staring at the ceiling, thinking about all the things I didn't get done that day, even though there's usually a pretty long list of things I didn't get done. And I don't wake up in the middle of the night, either. I sleep pretty soundly straight through until my alarm goes off at 6:00 AM. 

Sometimes I'll hit the snooze button once or twice, but that's just because I'm not really a morning person, not because I'm exhausted from tossing and turning all night. My husband actually jokes that I could sleep through a hurricane, which might be a bit of an exaggeration, but I definitely don't have insomnia or anything like that. So, no, my sleep is actually one of the few things that seems to be working exactly the way it's supposed to right now. It's just my waking hours that are the problem!
Do you have any physical complaints, such as headaches or stomach issues?

Headaches or stomach issues? No, thankfully no. Honestly, my physical health is... well, it's pretty robust, which is almost ironic when you think about how much my brain feels like it's just wandering off without my permission these days. But no, I don't get headaches. I know a lot of people in healthcare administration get terrible tension headaches from the stress—my sister actually gets migraines when she's overwhelmed—but I've never been prone to them at all. 

Even when I'm sitting there at my desk, staring at the exact same row of data for an hour because I keep losing my place and zoning out, I don't get a headache from it. Maybe my shoulders get a little stiff from hunching over my keyboard for too long, but that's just normal fifty-year-old stuff, you know? Not a real headache. And my stomach is completely fine. I have an iron stomach, really. I drink probably way too much coffee from the clinic breakroom, especially when I'm trying to force myself to stay alert during those long afternoon budget meetings, and it doesn't bother my digestion one bit. I never feel nauseous, no cramps, no acid reflux, nothing like that. 

It's actually kind of funny, you'd think with all this frustration I'm feeling about my lack of focus, it would show up physically somehow, like an ulcer or something. People always say stress carries in the body. But for me, it doesn't. My body is doing exactly what it's supposed to do, just like my sleep. It's really just my attention that's completely going rogue on me. So no, no physical complaints at all.
Do you have trouble remembering things that happened recently?

Remembering things? Like short-term memory? No, no, my memory is actually incredibly sharp. It’s funny you ask that, because my husband sometimes tries to tell me I have a memory problem when I don't pick up the dry cleaning on the way home, but I always have to correct him—I didn't forget, I just got completely derailed by something else before I could put it in my calendar! But as for actual memory, like recalling what happened yesterday or this morning? No, absolutely not. 

If you ask me what happened in the Tuesday morning huddle at the clinic, I can basically quote the charge nurse verbatim. I know exactly what we discussed during the compliance review last week, I remember conversations with my staff perfectly... I mean, I could probably tell you what everyone was wearing at the department head meeting yesterday. 

The problem isn't that I can't retrieve the information once it's actually in my head. My brain is like a steel trap for that kind of stuff. The real issue is just getting it into my brain in the first place. Like, if my mind is drifting—like I was describing earlier when I'm staring at those EPIC reports—well, obviously I can't remember what I didn't process because I was completely zoned out. But that's not a memory issue, you know? That's just me not being present. If I'm actually engaged and the information gets through, I remember it all perfectly. I can recall the exact phrasing a patient relations coordinator used in an email three days ago without even looking at my inbox. So, no, I wouldn't say I have any trouble with my memory at all. It's really just the staying tuned in part that's the struggle.
Do you find yourself easily distracted by your surroundings or thoughts when you're trying to focus?

Distracted by my surroundings? Gosh, I'm not entirely sure how to answer that. I mean, if you saw my office at the clinic, you'd think anyone would be distracted. I'm right down the hall from the main nurses' station, so there's always a constant hum of activity—call bells going off, the pneumatic tube system thunking, the medical assistants coming in and out, doctors debating with the pharmacy on the phone. It's Grand Central Station some days! 

But honestly? I haven't really noticed that the *environment* is what's pulling me away. It's not like I hear a conversation outside my door and suddenly I'm eavesdropping instead of doing my budget variance reports. So no, not the surroundings, I don't think. 

But then you mentioned thoughts... and that's where I get a little tripped up on what exactly counts as a distraction. Because, like I was telling you before about the zoning out... it's not always a specific thought that interrupts me. It's not like I'm sitting there and suddenly I think, 'Oh, I need to renew my car registration!' and then I lose my place. It's more like... a blankness? Or maybe just a very quiet drifting? I'll be staring at my monitor, and then ten minutes have gone by, and I couldn't even tell you what I was thinking about during that time. 

So I don't know if my own thoughts are distracting me, or if my attention just sort of... dissolves into thin air. What do you mean by distracted, exactly? Are you talking about actively thinking about other things, like daydreaming about a vacation, or just that feeling of not being present? Because if it's the active daydreaming part, I really haven't noticed that happening. I'm not sitting there entertaining myself with other ideas. It's really just that drifting feeling I mentioned before, where the focus just evaporates without me even realizing it's gone.
Do you ever feel mentally foggy or like you're in a daze when you're not zoning out?

Mentally foggy? Or in a daze? No, no, I wouldn't say that at all. It's really just that specific zooming-out thing I've been talking about. When I'm not doing that—when I'm actually present and engaged—my mind is completely clear. 

Like, if I'm in a fast-paced meeting, or if there's a minor crisis on the floor—say, the staffing coordinator calls out sick and I have to rearrange the schedule for three different departments by 8:00 AM—I am sharp as a tack. There's no fog. I'm firing on all cylinders, delegating tasks, making quick decisions... I feel completely alert. I don't walk around all day feeling groggy or like my head is stuffed with cotton, which is how my husband describes it when he takes those allergy pills in the spring. He gets so out of it he once put his keys in the refrigerator. I've never done anything like that. 

My baseline state, when I'm not staring at a spreadsheet and losing my grip on reality, is very lucid. I don't feel sluggish or confused. Even when I haven't slept perfectly—which is rare, because I'm a great sleeper, like I said—I still wake up feeling clear-headed. I get my coffee, I drive to work, I know exactly what my objectives for the day are. The clarity is there. 

It's really only when I have to sit down and do those monotonous, sustained tasks that the drifting happens. And even then, it's not a fog that settles over me, it's just... an absence of focus. Does that make sense? It's like a light switch. When it's on, the room is completely bright and I see everything perfectly. But when it flips off during those boring tasks, it's just... off. There's no dim, foggy middle ground where I'm stumbling around in a daze. So no, no mental fog at all.
Do you think your mind drifting away is related to the task being boring or uninteresting?

Well, boring is... I mean, yes, but it's more than just being bored. It's not like waiting in line at the DMV where you're just tapping your foot and wishing you were somewhere else. It's... it's the mental weight of it. 

Like, take the dense policy reviews I have to do. The hospital system is always updating compliance protocols, and as a manager, I have to read through these massive, dry documents and figure out how they apply to our specific clinics. Or the data-analysis blocks—looking at patient flow metrics, cross-referencing wait times with staffing levels over a quarter. I know I have to do them. I know they're important. But the thought of sitting down and actually forcing my brain to engage with that much detailed reading and... and intense, sustained thinking? It feels almost physically hard to start. 

I literally find myself putting those specific tasks off until late in the day. I'll come in at 8:00 AM, look at my to-do list, see "Review Q3 Compliance Updates," and I'll think, "Okay, I'll just clear out my inbox first." And then I'll reorganize my desk. And then I'll decide I need to go check on the front desk staff, which I don't really need to do right then, but I do it anyway. And then I'll handle a vendor issue, and then I'll eat lunch, and suddenly it's 4:00 PM and I still haven't opened the document. 

Because sitting down to do it just feels so... monumental. It's like standing at the bottom of a really steep hill and knowing you have to run up it, and you just keep finding reasons to stretch instead of starting the run. It takes so much effort to just lock my brain into that mode. So, yes, it's uninteresting, but it's really the amount of mental effort required that makes me avoid it like the plague. I'll do literally anything else—even dealing with an angry patient, which nobody likes—just to avoid that heavy, dense mental lifting.
Have you noticed any effects of your mind drifting away on your relationships with family or friends?

Family and friends? You know, honestly, not really. My husband is incredibly patient—well, except when I forget to add something to the grocery list, but that's just normal marriage stuff, right? And my friends, we mostly just do dinners or catch up over coffee, so there's not a lot of pressure or deadlines involved there. So, no, my personal relationships are mostly fine. 

But... where I *am* seeing a real impact—and this is honestly what has me so stressed out lately—is the professional side of things, and my community work. It's getting to be a real problem. At work, because of that whole cycle I was just describing—the putting off the heavy mental tasks and the drifting when I finally try to do them—my delays have actually started affecting the clinic's reporting deadlines. And that is so not like me. I'm a manager! I'm supposed to be the one keeping everyone else on track. But lately, I'm the bottleneck. I'm making other teams wait on me. The finance department will be waiting for my quarterly variance reports so they can finalize the regional budgets, or the compliance team is waiting on my audit reviews, and I'm just... stuck. I have the regional director emailing me, asking for updates, and it's mortifying because I know I'm holding up their entire workflow just because I can't force my brain to get through the paperwork.

And it's not just my paid job, either. It’s affecting my volunteer work, which really hurts. For years, I’ve been heavily involved in organizing these volunteer community health workshops—we do free blood pressure screenings, diabetes education, connecting uninsured folks with local resources, that sort of thing. It's wonderful work, and I usually lead a huge portion of the organizing committee. But recently... I actually had to step back from leading those parts. I had to call the board president and tell her I couldn't take it on this season. 

I just realized I can’t reliably keep all the planning pieces moving right now. There are so many logistical details to juggle—coordinating the volunteer nurses' schedules, securing the community center space, managing the donated supplies—and I knew that with the way my focus has just been dissolving into thin air, I was going to drop the ball. It broke my heart to step down, it really did, because I love that program and I've been doing it for so long, but I just couldn't trust myself to keep it all together and I didn't want the workshops to suffer because of me.
Do you ever feel restless or fidgety when you're trying to focus on a task?

Restless? Like, physically fidgety? No, I really wouldn't say so. It's actually almost the exact opposite. When I finally do force myself to sit down at my desk to tackle one of those heavy tasks—like the variance reports I was just mentioning—I am completely still. 

I have this ergonomic chair at the clinic, which we all got last year after this huge back-and-forth with the supplier because they kept sending the wrong lumbar specifications and the wrong fabric colors, but anyway, when I sit in it, I am planted. My feet are flat on the floor, my hands are resting on the keyboard, exactly how they teach you in those mandatory workplace safety modules. I don't bounce my leg. I don't click my pen incessantly. My nephew, who's in middle school, he does that—when he's at the dining table doing his math homework, his knee is going a mile a minute and he's constantly getting up to check the fridge or sharpen a pencil that doesn't need sharpening. 

I don't do any of that. I don't have this physical urge to get up and pace around my office or anything. There's no motor running inside me making me want to move. I can sit in that chair for forty-five minutes, completely like a statue, just staring at the computer screen. I'll just watch the cursor blinking on the spreadsheet. Blink, blink, blink. And if one of the charge nurses walked past my glass door, they would probably look in and think, wow, she is deep in concentration, she hasn't moved a muscle in half an hour. 

But in reality, my brain has completely checked out. I'm just sitting there, totally motionless, while my mind is off somewhere else entirely. I'm not physically uncomfortable or itching to jump out of my skin, I'm just... absent. So, no, there’s no physical restlessness or fidgeting at all. It’s entirely a mental drifting while my body just stays perfectly put.
Do you find it harder to focus on certain types of tasks than others?

Oh, absolutely. It's very specific things. And honestly, this exact issue is what finally pushed me to come in and see you in the first place. 

Because I can sit down to start an EPIC quality report—and you know EPIC, the electronic health record system we use, it's a beast on its own, especially since they updated the reporting dashboards last fall which added about fifteen new metrics we have to track for patient satisfaction and throughput and all of that. But anyway, I will sit down at my computer to start one of those reports, or I'll go sit down in a clinic metrics meeting in our main conference room, and I go in with every intention of tracking it. I really do. I have my notebook open, my pen ready, I tell myself, "Okay, focus, this is important for the quarterly review." 

But then, within just a few minutes... my mind has drifted so far away. It's like a fog just rolls in. I'll suddenly realize I've been staring at the screen, just rereading the exact same row of numbers on the report over and over again without actually processing what any of it means. I'm just looking at the digits. Or in the meeting, I'll kind of snap back to reality and realize the regional director is on the next slide and I completely missed the whole point of the discussion. I'll look around and think, wait, what did we just decide about the wait times? And I just have no idea. It's incredibly frustrating when you sit down actively trying to pay attention to these critical meetings and reports, and the information just slips right through your fingers anyway.
Do you find it harder to focus when you're at home compared to when you're at work?

Honestly? No, not really. I wish I could say it was just a work thing, or just a home thing, because then maybe I could just change my environment and fix it, right? But it's pretty much exactly the same no matter where I am. 

You would think home might be a little easier because it's my own space and I have total control over it. We live in this lovely little split-level that we bought about fifteen years ago, and I actually set up a really nice dedicated home office in the spare room downstairs. This was back during the pandemic when we all thought we'd be working from home forever. We painted it this very calming shade of sage green, got a nice solid oak desk, set up a really good filing system... the whole nine yards, specifically so I'd have a quiet, organized place to handle the household administration. You know, paying the bills, sorting through the mail, dealing with our own health insurance claims—which is ironic given what I do for a living! 

But even in that perfectly quiet, perfectly organized room, the exact same thing happens. I'll sit down on a Saturday morning with my coffee, I'll open up the electric bill, and I'll just... stare at it. I know I just need to log into the bank portal and schedule the payment. It takes maybe two minutes. But my mind just completely wanders off. I'll sit there looking at the little bar graph they put on the bill that shows your energy usage compared to last year, and I'll look at it for ten minutes without actually registering a single piece of information. I'm just looking at the little blue bars, completely zoned out. 

So, no, the location really doesn't seem to matter at all. Whether I'm sitting at my desk at the clinic with the phones ringing down the hall and the medical assistants walking by, or I'm sitting in my perfectly quiet home office... the fog just rolls in exactly the same way. It's incredibly frustrating, because it really doesn't seem to care what building I'm in.
Do you find that your ability to focus varies at different times of the day?

Time of the day? You know, I've actually tried to track that. Because my sister-in-law was telling me all about circadian rhythms and how everyone has a peak productivity window, usually between 9 AM and 11 AM, and she was saying I should just schedule all my heavy cognitive tasks for that window. She read this whole book about it, one of those self-help time-management books that are always on the bestseller lists at the airport. So I thought, okay, maybe that's my problem. Maybe I'm just trying to do the wrong things at the wrong time. 

So I really paid attention to it for a few weeks. I would get into the clinic around 7:30, before the phones start ringing, make my coffee—we have one of those commercial Keurig machines in the breakroom that the practice partners finally agreed to lease after complaining about the monthly cost for three years—and I would sit down at my desk feeling completely awake, completely rested. First cup of French roast in hand. You'd think that would be my prime time, right? But I'll open up the overnight census report, and the exact same thing happens. I just stare at it. The fog rolls in just as thick at 8:00 AM as it does at any other time. 

And then I thought, well, maybe I'm an afternoon person. Some people are afternoon people, right? But no, if I'm sitting in a 2:00 PM staffing meeting, right after lunch when people usually talk about having that afternoon slump, I'm drifting off in the exact same way. I mean, I'm not falling asleep, just... my mind is completely checking out, looking at the whiteboard without actually reading the words the clinical director is writing. 

And it's exactly the same in the evening at home. I could be sitting on the couch at 8:00 PM trying to read an article in a magazine, and I'll read the same paragraph six times without absorbing a single sentence. So, really, no. I haven't noticed any variation at all. Morning, noon, or night, before coffee, after coffee... it doesn't seem to make a bit of difference. The drifting just happens whenever I have to sit and focus, regardless of what the clock says.
Do you find it harder to focus on tasks that require a lot of mental calculation versus those that involve reading or understanding complex information?

Well, it's funny you ask it that way, comparing the math to the reading, because honestly, they both just feel like this massive mountain I have to climb. In my role as a clinic manager, I really have to do both constantly. I have these long data-analysis blocks where I have to look at budget variances and calculate FTE ratios for the nursing staff, which is very heavy on the numbers and the calculations. And then on the flip side, I have these incredibly dense policy reviews. Just last week, corporate sent down this revised compliance manual on telehealth billing codes that I was supposed to digest and summarize for the providers, which is purely reading and understanding complex rules. 

And what happens is, I find myself putting off both of those things. I will take the dense policy reviews and those long data-analysis blocks and I just keep pushing them back and pushing them back. I tell myself I will tackle them first thing, but then I find some minor email to answer instead, or I decide I absolutely need to organize my inbox folders right that second. So I end up putting them off until late in the day, usually right before I'm supposed to leave, which makes absolutely no sense because I'm already exhausted by then. 

But I do it because just the thought of sitting down with that much detailed reading and thinking... it feels almost physically hard to start. It is like there is an actual, physical weight pressing down on my chest when I look at the spreadsheet or the policy document. My brain just actively repels it. I will literally go out to the admin pod and restock the printer paper—which isn't even my job, the front desk coordinator usually handles the office supplies—just to avoid sitting down and initiating that heavy mental work. It doesn't really matter if it's calculating metrics or reading complex paragraphs, if it requires that deep, sustained effort, I just feel this intense physical resistance to even beginning the task, so I just keep kicking the can down the road until the sun goes down.
Do you find that your difficulty with focusing is limited to specific tasks or environments, or does it occur across a wide range of situations?

Well, like I was saying about the clinic versus the home office, and the math versus the reading... I really haven't noticed it being limited to anything specific at all. It just seems to happen everywhere, across a really wide range of situations. I honestly wish I could pinpoint just one or two triggers, because then maybe I could avoid them or work around them, you know? But it bleeds into literally every part of my life. 

Even things I actually want to do, which is the most baffling part to me. Like, my husband and I have this Sunday tradition where we watch these British murder mysteries on PBS. We've been watching them for years, it's our favorite way to unwind before the work week starts. We make a whole evening out of it, we brew a pot of Earl Grey tea, we get cozy on the couch... and I love these shows, I really do. But we'll be twenty minutes in, and suddenly I realize I haven't actually been paying attention to the screen for the last five minutes. My mind just completely floated away. I'll start thinking about whether I need to buy more furnace filters for the winter, or wondering what happened to the girl I sat next to in my freshman biology class in college, and meanwhile, a major plot point just happened on the TV. My husband has to pause the show—and bless his heart, he is so patient about it, but I know it has to drive him crazy—and he has to explain what just happened because I totally zoned out.

And it happens in social situations, too, which is just embarrassing. I have this monthly dinner club with some girlfriends, we usually go to this little Italian place downtown that makes their own pasta from scratch. It's a wonderful time, I look forward to it all month. But one of my oldest friends will be right in the middle of telling me a story, maybe about her daughter's wedding planning, and I'm making eye contact, I'm nodding, I'm smiling at the right times... but I am not actually taking in a single word she's saying. It's like the audio just cuts out and my brain is just... somewhere else entirely, completely detached from the conversation. 

So, no, it's definitely not just limited to heavy mental work or boring administrative tasks at the clinic. It's reading a book for pleasure, it's watching TV, it's trying to follow a conversation with a friend at dinner... I really haven't found a single environment or situation where that fog doesn't eventually roll in.
Do you find it easier to focus on tasks that you find interesting versus those that you don't?

You know, you would think that if I found something genuinely interesting, it would be a breeze. But like I was just mentioning with the PBS shows and the dinners with my girlfriends... those are things I truly love doing, things I look forward to all week, and I still just float away. So, no, interest doesn't really seem to be the magic shield I wish it was. 

And honestly, it's not even just about fun, leisurely things versus boring things. It happens with things I am deeply invested in professionally, too. In fact, that is exactly what finally pushed me to come in and make this appointment. I can sit down at my computer to start an EPIC quality report—and we actually just went through this massive, agonizing EPIC system upgrade last quarter, so these reports are highly scrutinized by the partners right now—or I'll sit down in a crucial clinic metrics meeting. And I go in with every intention of tracking it. I really do. I've got my legal pad, I know how important the data is, I am fully prepared to engage. 

But within just a few minutes, my mind has drifted so far off that I'll suddenly snap back and realize I'm just rereading the exact same row of numbers on the screen over and over again, or I'll tune back into the room and realize I completely missed the whole point of the discussion that the clinical director was just leading. And I built half of those reporting structures! I care about them! I want to know what's happening with our patient volume and our wait times. But my brain just goes on vacation without my permission, completely regardless of how interested I am or how much I want to pay attention. It's just making me feel like I'm losing my edge, which is terrifying when you're responsible for keeping a whole medical practice running smoothly.
Do you think your difficulty focusing is related to feeling overwhelmed or stressed about specific aspects of your life or work?

Well, it's interesting you bring up feeling overwhelmed, because... yes and no? I mean, I certainly *am* stressed, but the focus issues really started when the stress changed its shape, if that makes sense. If I really sit down and look back at the timeline of all this, I can trace it back to exactly two years and four months ago. 

That was right after our fiscal year ended, and the partners offered me a promotion to Regional Clinic Manager. Before that, I was just managing our main outpatient facility, and I was doing a great job! I had everything completely dialed in. I had my color-coded binders for different departments, I had this elaborate sticky note system framing my computer monitor, and I had my very specific routines, like checking in with the charge nurses every single morning at 8:15 sharp. I had all these little systems in place, and they worked beautifully for me for years. I never really noticed a problem with my focus because my environment was so tightly controlled.

But then I got this promotion, and suddenly my portfolio just exploded. Instead of just the one clinic, I was suddenly overseeing three different locations, including that new urgent care annex across town, which has completely different operating hours, a totally different staffing model, and a much higher patient turnover rate. 

And what happened was, that larger portfolio just completely started overwhelming the systems I used to rely on. It was like a dam breaking. My sticky notes weren't cutting it anymore because I wasn't sitting at the same desk every day—I was constantly driving between sites. The binders were way too heavy to lug back and forth in my car. I couldn't do my 8:15 check-ins because I might be at a completely different campus. And without all those old systems—which I guess I'm now realizing were actually massive crutches keeping me functioning—my brain just kind of short-circuited. 

So, yes, the overwhelm is absolutely there, but it's not just general life stress. This whole inability to stay on track has been going on specifically since that promotion two years and four months ago, because the sheer volume of the new role just broke every single workaround I had spent my entire career building up. It's like I could manage perfectly fine when the box was small enough, but once they made the box bigger, everything just fell completely apart.
Do you find that your difficulty focusing occurs with both simple and complex tasks?

Well, you know, I really haven't noticed if it's one or the other. I mean, I guess I'd have to sit down and really think about it to categorize what counts as a simple task versus a complex task in my day-to-day life right now, because honestly, everything just feels like a jumbled mess lately. Like, is approving a timecard a simple task? Because I used to just click through them on Friday afternoons while drinking my coffee, and now I stare at the screen and my mind wanders off to whether the landscaping crew has mulched the front beds at the urgent care center yet. I'm preoccupied, yes, but I'm preoccupied with fifty different things all at once, and none of them are the thing I'm actually supposed to be looking at or listening to in that exact moment. It's exhausting, really, because I feel like I'm thinking so hard all day long, but I'm just not thinking about the right things at the right time. So, I don't know if that completely answers your question, but it feels like a mix of both? My attention is there, it's just entirely hijacked by whatever random thought decides to parade through my head.

Time of the day? You know, I've actually tried to track that. Because my sister-in-law was telling me all about circadian rhythms and how everyone has a peak productivity window, usually between 9 AM and 11 AM, and she was saying I should just schedule all my heavy cognitive tasks for that window. She read this whole book about it, one of those self-help time-management books that are always on the bestseller lists at the airport. So I thought, okay, maybe that's my problem. Maybe I'm just trying to do the wrong things at the wrong time. 

So I really paid attention to it for a few weeks. I would get into the clinic around 7:30, before the phones start ringing, make my coffee—we have one of those commercial Keurig machines in the breakroom that the practice partners finally agreed to lease after complaining about the monthly cost for three years—and I would sit down at my desk feeling completely awake, completely rested. First cup of French roast in hand. You'd think that would be my prime time, right? But I'll open up the overnight census report, and the exact same thing happens. I just stare at it. The fog rolls in just as thick at 8:00 AM as it does at any other time. 

And then I thought, well, maybe I'm an afternoon person. Some people are afternoon people, right? But no, if I'm sitting in a 2:00 PM staffing meeting, right after lunch when people usually talk about having that afternoon slump, I'm drifting off in the exact same way. I mean, I'm not falling asleep, just... my mind is completely checking out, looking at the whiteboard without actually reading the words the clinical director is writing. 

And it's exactly the same in the evening at home. I could be sitting on the couch at 8:00 PM trying to read an article in a magazine, and I'll read the same paragraph six times without absorbing a single sentence. So, really, no. I haven't noticed any variation at all. Morning, noon, or night, before coffee, after coffee... it doesn't seem to make a bit of difference. The drifting just happens whenever I have to sit and focus, regardless of what the clock says.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's difficulty with focus is consistent across different types of mental tasks
doctor.question: Do you find it harder to focus on tasks that require a lot of mental calculation versus those that involve reading or understanding complex information?

target_item.name: Sustained_Mental_Effort_Avoidance
target_item.manifestation: I find myself putting off the dense policy reviews and long data-analysis blocks until late in the day, because the thought of sitting with that much detailed reading and thinking feels almost physically hard to start.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about tasks that require mental calculation or reading/understanding complex information, which directly relates to tasks requiring sustained mental effort. The patient's manifestation for S006 specifically mentions dense policy reviews and long data-analysis blocks.

patient.answer:
Well, it's funny you ask it that way, comparing the math to the reading, because honestly, they both just feel like this massive mountain I have to climb. In my role as a clinic manager, I really have to do both constantly. I have these long data-analysis blocks where I have to look at budget variances and calculate FTE ratios for the nursing staff, which is very heavy on the numbers and the calculations. And then on the flip side, I have these incredibly dense policy reviews. Just last week, corporate sent down this revised compliance manual on telehealth billing codes that I was supposed to digest and summarize for the providers, which is purely reading and understanding complex rules. 

And what happens is, I find myself putting off both of those things. I will take the dense policy reviews and those long data-analysis blocks and I just keep pushing them back and pushing them back. I tell myself I will tackle them first thing, but then I find some minor email to answer instead, or I decide I absolutely need to organize my inbox folders right that second. So I end up putting them off until late in the day, usually right before I'm supposed to leave, which makes absolutely no sense because I'm already exhausted by then. 

But I do it because just the thought of sitting down with that much detailed reading and thinking... it feels almost physically hard to start. It is like there is an actual, physical weight pressing down on my chest when I look at the spreadsheet or the policy document. My brain just actively repels it. I will literally go out to the admin pod and restock the printer paper—which isn't even my job, the front desk coordinator usually handles the office supplies—just to avoid sitting down and initiating that heavy mental work. It doesn't really matter if it's calculating metrics or reading complex paragraphs, if it requires that deep, sustained effort, I just feel this intense physical resistance to even beginning the task, so I just keep kicking the can down the road until the sun goes down.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's difficulty with focus is consistent across different environments and tasks, potentially indicating a more pervasive attention issue
doctor.question: Do you find that your difficulty with focusing is limited to specific tasks or environments, or does it occur across a wide range of situations?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking whether the focusing difficulties occur across multiple settings or situations, which corresponds to the DSM-5 criterion for symptoms being present in two or more settings. This specific criterion is not in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Well, like I was saying about the clinic versus the home office, and the math versus the reading... I really haven't noticed it being limited to anything specific at all. It just seems to happen everywhere, across a really wide range of situations. I honestly wish I could pinpoint just one or two triggers, because then maybe I could avoid them or work around them, you know? But it bleeds into literally every part of my life. 

Even things I actually want to do, which is the most baffling part to me. Like, my husband and I have this Sunday tradition where we watch these British murder mysteries on PBS. We've been watching them for years, it's our favorite way to unwind before the work week starts. We make a whole evening out of it, we brew a pot of Earl Grey tea, we get cozy on the couch... and I love these shows, I really do. But we'll be twenty minutes in, and suddenly I realize I haven't actually been paying attention to the screen for the last five minutes. My mind just completely floated away. I'll start thinking about whether I need to buy more furnace filters for the winter, or wondering what happened to the girl I sat next to in my freshman biology class in college, and meanwhile, a major plot point just happened on the TV. My husband has to pause the show—and bless his heart, he is so patient about it, but I know it has to drive him crazy—and he has to explain what just happened because I totally zoned out.

And it happens in social situations, too, which is just embarrassing. I have this monthly dinner club with some girlfriends, we usually go to this little Italian place downtown that makes their own pasta from scratch. It's a wonderful time, I look forward to it all month. But one of my oldest friends will be right in the middle of telling me a story, maybe about her daughter's wedding planning, and I'm making eye contact, I'm nodding, I'm smiling at the right times... but I am not actually taking in a single word she's saying. It's like the audio just cuts out and my brain is just... somewhere else entirely, completely detached from the conversation. 

So, no, it's definitely not just limited to heavy mental work or boring administrative tasks at the clinic. It's reading a book for pleasure, it's watching TV, it's trying to follow a conversation with a friend at dinner... I really haven't found a single environment or situation where that fog doesn't eventually roll in.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's difficulty with focus is consistent across different levels of interest in the task
doctor.question: Do you find it easier to focus on tasks that you find interesting versus those that you don't?

target_item.name: Sustained_Attention_Difficulty
target_item.manifestation: What finally pushed me to come in is that I can start an EPIC quality report or sit down in a clinic metrics meeting with every intention of tracking it, and within a few minutes my mind has drifted so far that I’m rereading the same numbers or realizing I missed the whole point of the discussion.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the ability to focus on interesting tasks versus uninteresting ones, which directly corresponds to the symptom of having difficulty sustaining attention in tasks or play activities.

patient.answer:
You know, you would think that if I found something genuinely interesting, it would be a breeze. But like I was just mentioning with the PBS shows and the dinners with my girlfriends... those are things I truly love doing, things I look forward to all week, and I still just float away. So, no, interest doesn't really seem to be the magic shield I wish it was. 

And honestly, it's not even just about fun, leisurely things versus boring things. It happens with things I am deeply invested in professionally, too. In fact, that is exactly what finally pushed me to come in and make this appointment. I can sit down at my computer to start an EPIC quality report—and we actually just went through this massive, agonizing EPIC system upgrade last quarter, so these reports are highly scrutinized by the partners right now—or I'll sit down in a crucial clinic metrics meeting. And I go in with every intention of tracking it. I really do. I've got my legal pad, I know how important the data is, I am fully prepared to engage. 

But within just a few minutes, my mind has drifted so far off that I'll suddenly snap back and realize I'm just rereading the exact same row of numbers on the screen over and over again, or I'll tune back into the room and realize I completely missed the whole point of the discussion that the clinical director was just leading. And I built half of those reporting structures! I care about them! I want to know what's happening with our patient volume and our wait times. But my brain just goes on vacation without my permission, completely regardless of how interested I am or how much I want to pay attention. It's just making me feel like I'm losing my edge, which is terrifying when you're responsible for keeping a whole medical practice running smoothly.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's difficulty with focus is related to stress or emotional state
doctor.question: Do you think your difficulty focusing is related to feeling overwhelmed or stressed about specific aspects of your life or work?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on since my promotion about two years and four months ago, when the larger portfolio started overwhelming the systems I used to rely on.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the difficulty focusing is related to feeling overwhelmed at work, which perfectly matches the patient's manifestation for duration, where she explains the issues started 2 years and 4 months ago when a promotion and larger portfolio started overwhelming her systems.

patient.answer:
Well, it's interesting you bring up feeling overwhelmed, because... yes and no? I mean, I certainly *am* stressed, but the focus issues really started when the stress changed its shape, if that makes sense. If I really sit down and look back at the timeline of all this, I can trace it back to exactly two years and four months ago. 

That was right after our fiscal year ended, and the partners offered me a promotion to Regional Clinic Manager. Before that, I was just managing our main outpatient facility, and I was doing a great job! I had everything completely dialed in. I had my color-coded binders for different departments, I had this elaborate sticky note system framing my computer monitor, and I had my very specific routines, like checking in with the charge nurses every single morning at 8:15 sharp. I had all these little systems in place, and they worked beautifully for me for years. I never really noticed a problem with my focus because my environment was so tightly controlled.

But then I got this promotion, and suddenly my portfolio just exploded. Instead of just the one clinic, I was suddenly overseeing three different locations, including that new urgent care annex across town, which has completely different operating hours, a totally different staffing model, and a much higher patient turnover rate. 

And what happened was, that larger portfolio just completely started overwhelming the systems I used to rely on. It was like a dam breaking. My sticky notes weren't cutting it anymore because I wasn't sitting at the same desk every day—I was constantly driving between sites. The binders were way too heavy to lug back and forth in my car. I couldn't do my 8:15 check-ins because I might be at a completely different campus. And without all those old systems—which I guess I'm now realizing were actually massive crutches keeping me functioning—my brain just kind of short-circuited. 

So, yes, the overwhelm is absolutely there, but it's not just general life stress. This whole inability to stay on track has been going on specifically since that promotion two years and four months ago, because the sheer volume of the new role just broke every single workaround I had spent my entire career building up. It's like I could manage perfectly fine when the box was small enough, but once they made the box bigger, everything just fell completely apart.

patient.answer:
Well, you know, I really haven't noticed if it's one or the other. I mean, I guess I'd have to sit down and really think about it to categorize what counts as a simple task versus a complex task in my day-to-day life right now, because honestly, everything just feels like a jumbled mess lately. Like, is approving a timecard a simple task? Because I used to just click through them on Friday afternoons while drinking my coffee, and now I stare at the screen and my mind wanders off to whether the landscaping crew has mulched the front beds at the urgent care center yet. And then, of course, the complex tasks, like the budget forecasting for the next fiscal year across all three sites... that's definitely complex, and I struggle with that too, but is it the complexity itself that's the issue, or is it just the fact that it's a task in front of me? 

I really don't know if I can draw a clear line between the two. Sometimes I feel like making a grocery list is just as impossible as drafting a quarterly performance review for one of my department heads. It's like the gears just get stuck, regardless of whether it's a tiny little gear or a massive, complicated one. I just... I haven't really been able to spot a pattern where one type of task is definitely worse than the other. They both just seem to slip away from me before I even realize what's happening.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's difficulty focusing is more related to attention deficit or another condition
doctor.question: Do you think your mind drifting away is more due to not being able to pay attention or because you're preoccupied with other thoughts?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking to differentiate whether the inattention is due to an inability to focus or preoccupation with other thoughts (often to rule out anxiety or depression), which does not map to a specific symptom in the provided profile.

patient.answer:
Well, that's... gosh, that's a really good question, and honestly, I've spent a lot of time trying to untangle that exact thing in my own head. Is it that I can't focus, or is it that I'm focusing on the wrong things? Because it feels like my brain is just constantly running on a treadmill, but the treadmill is in the wrong room. 

Like, if I'm sitting in one of those clinic metrics meetings I mentioned—the ones with the clinical director where I just completely lose the thread—I'm not sitting there staring blankly at the wall with an empty head. My mind isn't a void. It's actually incredibly busy. I'll be looking right at the slide showing the patient wait times for the urgent care annex, and suddenly I'm thinking about whether we ordered enough of the pediatric flu swabs for the upcoming season, which reminds me that the supply closet on the second floor of the main clinic has a broken hinge on the door, which reminds me that I need to call facilities, which reminds me that the facilities manager's wife just had a baby and I should probably get a card for the team to sign... and by the time I snap back to reality, the clinical director is three slides ahead, talking about billing codes, and I have absolutely no idea how we got there.

So I guess I wouldn't say it's just a pure inability to pay attention, like a light switch being flipped off. It's more like... like a radio that keeps scanning for a new station on its own. I'm preoccupied, yes, but I'm preoccupied with fifty different things all at once, and none of them are the thing I'm actually supposed to be looking at or listening to in that exact moment. It's exhausting, really, because I feel like I'm thinking so hard all day long, but I'm just not thinking about the right things at the right time. So, I don't know if that completely answers your question, but it feels like a mix of both? My attention is there, it's just entirely hijacked by whatever random thought decides to parade through my head.
